newsitem.title: USA: Need inflation proof? Take me out to the ballgame.
newsitem.headline: Need inflation proof? Take me out to the ballgame.

text.p: Federal Reserve policymakers can talk all they want about how inflation remains tame with little pressures in the pipeline.

But maybe they should take in a ballgame and see for themselves how sports ticket prices have soared at more than twice the overall inflation rate in recent years, and there's no sign of that stopping.

"Prices are just outrageous," said Barbara Bernard, who analyzes ticket prices in the entertainment and sports industries at the Bureau of Labor Statistics. "It's amazing what I see come across my desk."
Yet, she added, "They get away with it, especially the more popular teams who can get away with practically anything."

Bernard noted that prices are not just rising among professional teams. High school and college sports ticket prices are creeping up, too, as "municipalities tighten their belts and don't give as much subsidies to schools."
The surge in sports ticket prices, though, is not reflected much in the Consumer Price Index (CPI), given that it accounts for only 0.7 percent of the entire CPI.
While overall consumer inflation has risen between 2.5 and 3.3 percent over the past four years, sports ticket prices have skyrocketed as much as 10 percent year-over-year.
"As people have become better off they spend a larger proportion of their income on leisure time pursuits," said Roger McCain, economics professor at Drexel University.

According to the Chicago-based Team Marketing Report, prices at Major League Baseball Games rose 7.1 percent in the 1997 season over 1996. Similarly, professional basketball ticket prices were up 8.0 percent this past season, while professional football game prices rose 6.6 percent.
Hockey ticket prices chalked up the biggest increases of the major sports leagues this year, rising 10.3 percent.

But attendance figures have not suffered. Despite an average rise of more than 6.0 percent a year over the past few years for all major sports, attendance has been flat to a bit higher, the only exception being the year of the baseball strike in 1995.

"Sports teams are all monopolies, which restrict the growth of franchises so it doesn't keep up with the growth in demand," said Andrew Zimbalist, a professor of economics at Smith College. "There is always more excess demand."
At the same time, new state-of-the-art ballparks and arenas are being built, while players' salaries reach astronomical proportions, with no signs of letting up.
"Those are being reflected in the price of a ticket," Bernard of the BLS said.
Robert Frank, author of the book "Winner Take All Society," noted that teams do get some revenues from television contracts which offsets the price of a ticket to some degree.

"Teams don't raise prices more than the market will bear," said Frank, a professor of economics at Cornell University's Johnson School of Management. "If the time comes and people start staying home, that will be a signal for prices to moderate."
But based on data, the hefty rises in ticket prices have not stopped millions and millions of fans from heading to the ballpark or arena each year.
Zimbalist attributed that to steady ticket prices at the lower end of the price scale, even as higher end prices have risen quickly along with demand from corporations for luxury box seats.
Fans who wish to spend less can go to minor league games, which have done very well in recent years by keeping prices of tickets, hot dogs and parking down.
Yet, economists said, it's just not the same as the pros.
"People have a hunger for players with true star power," Frank said. "Everyone wants to see (Chicago Bulls basketball great) Michael Jordan."
And since team management understand this, analysts said, higher prices will stick much more than increases at the supermarket and gas station.

Unlike other items, sports is "more insulated" from day-to-day competition, Frank said. "You can't import cheap baseball from Korea if American baseball gets too expensive. But if American cars get too expensive, you can buy a (less expensive) car from Korea."
